Background Although direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) have revolutionized the management of chronic HCV, the debatable association with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) occurrence/recurrence has raised major concerns about their long-term use, especially in cirrhotic cases. The role of epithelial tight junction proteins (TJPs) in hepatocarcinogenesis has been highlighted; however, the association of their expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) with HCC has rarely been reported. This study aimed to explore the role of peripheral claudin (Cldn) 1 in liver pathogenesis and its crosstalk with soluble immune mediators in HCC prognosis. Methods The study population included six independent subgroups: healthy controls, cirrhotic/non-cirrhotic treatment-naïve HCV patients, DAA-SVR patients, and anticancer treatment-naïve de novo HCC patients. The laboratory tests included serum levels of alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), albumin, liver transaminases, total bilirubin, and CBC profiling. The serum levels of soluble cluster of differentiation (sCD)163, IL-10, and IL-12 were estimated by corresponding ELISA kits, whereas the levels of Cldn1 and transforming growth factor ( TGF )- β in PBMCs were quantified using quantitative PCR (qPCR). Results Serum sCD163, IL-10, and IL-12 levels were significantly higher in the HCC patient group than in the control and non-malignant patient groups ( P < 0.0001). No significant difference was detected in the serum levels of the three markers between cirrhotic and non-cirrhotic patients of chronic HCV, whereas their levels were significantly different between cirrhotic and non-cirrhotic SVRs ( P < 0.0001). Similarly, the transcriptional levels of peripheral Cldn1 and TGF-β were significantly higher in patients with HCC and non-malignant cirrhosis than in patients without cirrhosis ( P = 0.0185–<0.0001 and 0.0089–<0.0001, respectively). Logistic regression analysis revealed a significant association between all the abovementioned markers and HCC ( P = 0.0303 to < 0.0001), which was further confirmed by the results of receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, which revealed an area under the curve (AUC) value ranging from 0.883 to 0.996. The calculated cutoff values demonstrated remarkable prognostic capacity, with ranges of 88–99.41% and 82.14–97.92% and positive/negative predictive values ranging from 84.62 to 98.3% and 92–98%, respectively. Conclusion Serum sCD163, IL-10, IL-12 and peripheral Cldn1 and TGF-β expression levels represent novel non-invasive HCC biomarkers that maintain their predictive power under different pathological conditions and circumvent the drawbacks of conventional prognostic markers in patients with mild cirrhosis and/or normal AFP, albumin, and/or platelet counts. Keywords HCV-related HCC DAA Claudin sCD163 Cytokines Tight junction proteins National Research Centre Egypt Open access funding provided by The Science, Technology & Innovation Funding Authority (STDF) in cooperation with The Egyptian Knowledge Bank (EKB). issue-copyright-statement © BioMed Central Ltd., part of Springer Nature 2024 Introduction The burden of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is increasing worldwide as the third leading cause of cancer-related deaths, accounting for 90% of primary liver cancers and 8.3% of all cancer-associated mortalities, particularly among elderly people [ 1 ]. Several risk factors have been associated with HCC, including long-term exposure to fungal aflatoxins, smoking, alcohol abuse, metabolic diseases such as diabetes mellitus, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), and chronic viral infections such as hepatitis B (HBV) and C (HCV) viruses [ 2 ]. In particular, HCV remains the most common cause, and in addition to underlying cirrhosis as a key precursor of HCC, viral antigens can induce several protumorigenic mechanisms, including persistent oxido-inflammatory-mediated liver damage and dysregulation of cellular signaling pathways [ 3 ]. Evidently, chronic HCV infection can be efficiently treated with direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) that achieve a sustained virologic response (SVR) in > 95% of patients, improving extra-hepatic manifestations and “presumably” reducing the risk of cirrhosis-associated HCC [ 4 ]. However, several clinical studies and real-life experiences have revealed that the subsequent complications and risk of HCC are not entirely eliminated in all recovered patients, especially in cirrhotic patients [ 5 – 9 ]. One reason for this could be related to the persistence of HCV biological imprints after SVR, including virus-induced epigenetic changes in the liver associated with HCC development [ 10 ]. Another possible explanation is that cirrhosis-induced alterations in the immune milieu are exacerbated by the introduction of DAAs and are similarly associated with a greater risk of HCC [ 11 ]. Considering the recent debate about the correlation between DAA-based therapy and HCC occurrence/recurrence [ 12 ] and the launching of nationwide surveillance programms for HCC in Egypt resembling those previously adopted for the testing and treatment of HCV [ 13 ], long-term follow-up for cirrhotic patients receiving DAAs is highly recommended. Typically, HCC prognosis and/or diagnosis often depend on several clinicopathological criteria, including tumor number, size, and focality; lymphovascular invasion, and pathological grade and stage [ 14 ]. In addition, the serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) level has long been a less invasive gold standard predictor of HCC [ 15 ]; however, the reliability of AFP may be compromised in patients with normal serum AFP levels, including HCC patients [ 16 ] and non-malignant cirrhotic patients [ 17 ], which necessitates the combination of other serum markers and imaging modalities [ 18 ]. Because HCC is an inflammation-induced cancer [ 19 ], various soluble immune mediators have been proposed as potential biomarkers for HCC prognosis, given their regulatory role in the host antitumor immune response, which determines the overall fate of tumorigenesis [ 20 ]. The tumor microenvironment (TME) is dominated by immunosuppressive cytokines that curtail the effector antitumor immune response and promote the survival and proliferation of tumor cells. Among these factors, transforming growth factor (TGF)-β and IL-10 are key players in HCC pathogenesis, where dysregulated TGF-β signaling pathways promote persistent liver inflammation, fibrogenesis, and TME immunomodulation [ 21 ]. Moreover, intrahepatic expression of the M2 cytokine IL-10 is the main modulator of liver fibrinogenesis during chronic infection [ 22 ] and one of the main precursors of HCC through genetic polymorphisms [ 23 ], which also contributes to perpetuating immunosuppressive conditions in the TME [ 20 , 21 ]. Similarly, soluble CD163 (sCD163), a specific biomarker for M2 macrophage activation, has been reported to play a key role in liver pathogenesis by activating several immunoregulatory pathways and therefore was introduced as a useful tool for assessing the severity of liver damage and predicting HCC [ 24 ]. Although chronic inflammation induced by several proinflammatory mediators has recently been identified as a co-factor in carcinogenesis [ 25 ], the pleiotropic cytokine IL-12 plays an essential role in inflammation-associated tumorigenesis, despite its classical role in activating cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) and natural killer (NK) cells for tumor clearance [ 26 ]. In addition, tight junction proteins (TJPs) have been shown to play multiple roles in liver pathogenesis, ranging from viral entry to cancer progression and metastasis, by promoting epithelial–mesenchymal transition [ 27 ] and have therefore become important therapeutic targets for liver cirrhosis and carcinoma [ 28 ]. In a recent study, Roehlen et al. [ 29 ] proposed that epithelial Cldn1 expressed on hepatocytes acts as a therapeutic target through specific antibodies that suppress protumorigenic cellular signaling and reprogram the TME [ 29 ]. Considering that blood samples are less invasive and easier to retrieve than tumor tissues are, peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) could be an excellent alternative for tumor surveillance, especially because their transcriptome is of single origin and can efficiently reflect local immune cell infiltration in the TME [ 30 ]. Nonetheless, to our knowledge, only one machine learning-based study has recently investigated peripheral TJP transcription in liver cancer [ 31 ]. In this study, we aimed to explore the role of peripheral Cldn1 expressed in PBMCs in liver pathogenesis and its crosstalk with soluble immune mediators in HCC prognosis.

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: Hepatocarcinogenesis, HCC development and progression, and liver tumorigenesis across varying stages of chronic HCV-related liver disease (cirrhosis, non-cirrhosis, SVR status, post-DAA treatment), encompassing differential expression of serum biomarkers and gene transcription in PBMCs.
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: Hepatocarcinogenesis is driven by dysregulated TGF-β signaling, promoting liver inflammation, fibrogenesis, and immunomodulation within the tumor microenvironment (TME). Intrahepatic IL-10 modulates liver fibrinogenesis during chronic infection, acts as an HCC precursor through genetic polymorphisms, and perpetuates immunosuppressive conditions in the TME, potentially also playing an immune-homeostatic role under hyperinflammation. sCD163 activates immunoregulatory pathways and promotes liver cirrhosis by activating hepatic Kupffer cells that overexpress IL-10. IL-12 plays a critical role in inflammation-associated tumorigenesis. Tight junction proteins (TJPs), particularly peripheral Cldn1 expressed in PBMCs, contribute to liver pathogenesis from viral entry to cancer progression and metastasis by promoting epithelial–mesenchymal transition. Cldn1 on hepatocytes has been proposed as a therapeutic target by suppressing protumorigenic cellular signaling and reprogramming the TME. The interplay between intrahepatic IL-10 and TGF-β determines fibrogenic severity in chronic HCV, directly relating to HCC development and progression. While viral elimination with DAA treatment improves outcomes, it can also lead to an upregulation of immunoregulatory mediators and/or growth factors, such as vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), and changes in the T-cell-mediated immunological milieu, potentially favoring HCC development due to reduced antitumor immune surveillance, though the precise oncogenic programming post-SVR remains unclear. The identified differential expression of serum sCD163, IL-10, IL-12, and transcriptional levels of Cldn1 and TGF-β in PBMCs are significantly associated with an increased risk of HCC.

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: The study detailed a DAA regimen (12-week sofosbuvir with or without ribavirin) and classifications of liver disease stages. Significant differences in biomarker levels were observed across patient groups: serum sCD163, IL-10, and IL-12 showed no significant difference between cirrhotic and non-cirrhotic chronic HCV patients, but were significantly different (P < 0.0001) between cirrhotic and non-cirrhotic SVRs. Specifically, sCD163 levels were 1.9-fold higher in cirrhotic SVRs and 1.23-fold higher in cirrhotic chronic patients compared to their non-cirrhotic counterparts. IL-12 levels in cirrhotic SVRs were also higher than in non-cirrhotic SVRs (P < 0.0001). Transcriptional levels of peripheral Cldn1 and TGF-β were significantly higher in patients with HCC and non-malignant cirrhosis than in patients without cirrhosis (P = 0.0185 –<0.0001 and 0.0089 –<0.0001, respectively). While Cldn1 and TGF-β levels in PBMCs of chronic HCV cirrhotic patients did not significantly differ from non-cirrhotic, non-cirrhotic SVR patients showed significantly lower expression of both genes compared to cirrhotic SVR patients (P = 0.0003 and P < 0.0001, respectively). HCC patients exhibited the highest frequencies of hypertension (66%, P < 0.0001) and diabetes mellitus (38%, P = 0.0026), and significantly higher median age than controls (P < 0.0001). HCC tumor aggressiveness was noted with 70% BCLC stage C and 50% having tumor maximum diameters of 3-10 cm. Cirrhotic patients, regardless of HCV or SVR status, showed significant reduction in PLT count and higher INRs compared to non-cirrhotic groups (P < 0.0001). AST levels and AST/ALT ratio were significantly higher in cirrhotic patients within non-malignant groups. HCC patients displayed significantly higher FIB-4 and Child –Pugh scores and AFP levels, but lower ALB levels, compared to non-malignant patients (P < 0.0001 for each). AFP levels in SVRs were significantly lower than in treatment-naïve HCV patients, even those with cirrhosis. Circulating levels of sCD163, IL-10 (up to 3.78-fold), and IL-12 (up to 13.83-fold) were notably higher in HCC patients compared to control and non-malignant cohorts. IL-12 levels were lower in chronic HCV patients, possibly due to viral core protein inhibition.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: sCD163 is a specific biomarker for M2 macrophage activation. The identified biomarkers (sCD163, IL-10, IL-12, Cldn1, TGF-β) demonstrate differential expression across various patient groups (control, non-malignant, cirrhotic, non-cirrhotic, HCC, SVR, chronic HCV), indicating specificity to disease stage and condition, particularly in association with HCC risk in cirrhotic patients. These markers circumvent the drawbacks of conventional prognostic markers like AFP, albumin, and platelet counts in patients with mild cirrhosis and/or normal levels of these conventional markers. They maintain a consistent pattern of association across different clinical markers and patient cohorts, confirming their predictive power under diverse pathological conditions. Significant changes in hematological and biochemical markers (RBCs, PLT, INRs, ALT, AST, AST/ALT ratio, BiL, FIB-4, Child-Pugh, AFP, ALB) were specifically associated with the presence and severity of HCC and with the stage of liver damage. Upregulation of CD163-expressing tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) was reported in HCC patients with poorly differentiated tumors and those with tumor sizes ">= 3.5 cm. The study notes that AFP's utility as a gold standard for HCC prognosis is compromised in cirrhotic DAA-SVRs with normal serum AFP levels, despite other indicators of liver damage. Contrast-enhanced MRI and CT were used for HCC diagnosis per AASLD/EASL guidelines, and FIB-4 cutoff values were utilized for assessing advanced fibrosis.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: Healthy controls, patients with chronic liver disease, specifically cirrhotic and non-cirrhotic Egyptian HCV patients (treatment-naïve and DAA-SVRs), anticancer treatment-naïve de novo HCC patients, non-malignant cirrhotic patients, and patients with mild cirrhosis and/or normal levels of conventional markers (AFP, albumin, platelet counts). The study included patients with Child-Pugh class A or B with compensated liver disease, or those in stable clinical conditions within 12 months after a history of decompensation.
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: The findings indicate significant alterations in hematological and biochemical profiles, liver function tests, and liver damage scores in HCC patients and those with advanced liver disease (cirrhosis). These changes suggest utility in the assessment of liver health, diagnosis of HCC, and evaluation of disease severity, particularly concerning the risk of hepatocarcinogenesis, HCC prognosis, and early prediction of HCC. The study highlights increased risk of HCC development and progression, the perpetuation of an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, liver damage, and fibrogenic severity. A higher frequency of hypertension and diabetes mellitus is noted among HCC patients. Additionally, it addresses concerns regarding reduced antitumor immune surveillance potentially leading to HCC development after DAA treatment and implications for mortality in patients with decompensated liver cirrhosis. There's also a potential immune-homeostatic role for IL-10 in halting liver damage under hyperinflammation.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: The identified biomarkers provide diagnostic utility for HCC and liver disease severity, and prognostic utility for HCC development, progression, and mortality in decompensated liver cirrhosis. They represent novel non-invasive HCC biomarkers with remarkable prognostic capacity. Adverse risk for HCC and liver complications is indicated by lower Red Blood Corpuscles (RBCs) and Platelet (PLT) counts, higher International Normalized Ratios (INRs), elevated AST, ALT, AST/ALT ratio, total bilirubin, FIB-4 scores, Child-Pugh scores, and AFP levels, coupled with lower albumin levels, particularly in HCC and cirrhotic patient populations. High levels of sCD163, IL-10, IL-12, peripheral Cldn1, and TGF-β are also associated with increased HCC risk. The study also utilizes established classifications like Child-Pugh score, ECOG Performance score, Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer (BCLC) staging, and FIB-4 for fibrosis risk assessment.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: The identified biomarkers (sCD163, IL-10, IL-12, Cldn1, and TGF-β mRNA expression) consistently demonstrated remarkable prognostic capacity for HCC risk and progression. Their performance was assessed through ROC analysis, revealing significant AUC values ranging from 0.7708 to 0.9969 (P = 0.0007 –<0.0001), with high sensitivity (82 –100%), specificity (86 –98%), positive predictive values (84.62 –98.3%), and negative predictive values (92 –98%). These markers presented larger AUROCs and higher sensitivity/specificity (88 –99.41% and 82.14 –97.92%, respectively) compared to traditional markers. They maintain their predictive power under different pathological conditions and circumvent the drawbacks of conventional prognostic markers such as AFP, albumin, and platelet counts, which often show suboptimal performance and are deemed unreliable in patients with mild fibrotic grades or normal levels. Serum albumin, in particular, showed the least predictive power among the tested markers. Methods contributing to reliability included viral load quantification via qPCR (LOD 21 IU/mL), triplicate assays for biochemical, immunological, and molecular assessments, use of GAPDH as a housekeeping gene, and melting curve analysis to confirm specific amplification. Statistical power calculation (0.9552 for AST/ALT ratio) was performed for the study design. However, the study acknowledges a limitation due to a small sample size, recommending further validation with larger cohorts.
